subject: physics
title: Quantum & Nuclear Physics (HL) Adventure 3: Binding energy curve and reactions
welcome_lead: Today you'll plot the binding energy curve and calculate ΔE in nuclear reactions.
meta_desc: Physics HL — binding energy per nucleon, Δm·c², fission energy, fusion energy, BE curve.
final_note: You learned BE/nucleon peaks at ⁵⁶Fe (~8.8 MeV); ΔE = Δm c² from mass defect; fission releases ~200 MeV, fusion ~17.6 MeV per reaction.

walkthroughs.body_html:
To split a nucleus into separate nucleons requires binding energy BE.

BE = Δm · c², where Δm = (sum of separated nucleons' mass) − (nucleus mass).

Divide by A to get BE/nucleon: average stability.

BE/nucleon vs A:

- Rises rapidly from H (0 MeV/nucleon) to ⁵⁶Fe (~8.8 MeV/nucleon, peak).
- Slowly falls for heavier.
- Light isotopes (²H, ³He) are below peak — fuse to release energy.
- Heavy isotopes (²³⁵U, ²³⁹Pu) — fission releases energy.

1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV/c².

Convert Δm in u directly to energy in MeV by × 931.5.

Example: ²³⁵U fission has Δm ≈ 0.215 u → 200 MeV. About 8.4 × 10¹⁰ J/g.

D + T fusion: Δm ≈ 0.0189 u → 17.6 MeV. ~3.4 × 10¹¹ J/g — even more energy-dense.

mcqs.q: Why is gravitational potential energy near a planet treated as negative?
options: Gravitational potential energy is negative because gravity always points downwards.
Gravitational potential energy is negative because gravity does negative work.
Because the zero is defined at infinity; objects bound to the planet have lower (negative) potential energy than at infinity.
Yes, but only in cities with old buildings.

mcqs.q: What is required to induce an emf in a coil using a magnet?
options: Gravitational potential energy is negative because gravity does negative work.
A changing magnetic flux linkage through the coil — the magnet (or coil) must be moving or the field must be changing.
A current in the coil is what induces an emf in the magnet.
Just having a magnet near the coil induces an emf, even when both are stationary.
